name: Kotoko (Kousseri)
parler: Kotoko (lagwan); Shuwa Arabic as a vehicular language
place: First-degree sultanate of Kousseri (Logone-et-Chari, Far North)
overview: Founders of Kousseri and guardians of its traditions, the Kotoko (Mantagé) say they are descended from the Sao, who came from ancient Egypt via Sudan and Chad. Under the authority of a sultan surrounded by notables, this people of Logone fishermen honours the water spirits, builds dugout canoes and dances to the sound of the sultan's drums.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Large group, mixed with the Massa, Mousgoum and other peoples of the town, to the point that it becomes difficult to tell them apart.
Shuwa Arabic serves as an indispensable vehicular language; Kotoko is also spoken at Magba and Lagdo.
Formerly mostly endogamous, the Kotoko today marry freely, men and women alike.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: First occupants and founders of Kousseri, they consider themselves the guardians of the town's traditions.
Having come from ancient Egypt via Sudan and Chad, they regard the Kotoko cities of neighbouring countries as their own.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A first-degree sultan leads the group, surrounded by notable-advisers and the three canton chiefs, whom he consults before announcing a decision.
The eldest son inherits, whatever his mother's clan.
Unmarried people of both sexes do not interact in public; relations with in-laws are free.
Conflicts between groups are settled by the arbitration of a patriarch; with Islam, the old rules of deference count for less.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's home.
A boy becomes a man when he can cultivate his plot alone. Ages given: 20 to 25 for the man, 18 for the woman.
To judge whether a young girl was ready, she was made to sit on the village's big mortar: if her feet touched the ground, she could marry.
Steps: request to the parents, then setting the date of the engagement.
The bride price is essential: the kola announces that the girl is promised, the néné (a set of gifts) is accepted by her as a sign of love, money seals the union.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cult of the water spirits: a black sheep is sacrificed to obtain an abundant catch and a safe crossing.
The appearance of the monitor lizard announces an event in the sultanate.
Symbolic places: the sultan's palace and its courtyard, the goudi (a pyramidal building that preserves the traditions), the banks of the Logone, the Sao-Kotoko museum in Kousseri.
Birth is celebrated with a baptism; “God created death before life”.
Murder is referred to State justice; adultery brings a heavy fine.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Activities: fishing, farming, market gardening.
The land belongs to the sultan; in the division, the man receives twice as much as the woman.
Ancestral crafts: weaving, doors, dugout canoes (zemi), boney hat worn with the grand boubou.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Woven clothing (gabaga), gandoura; the woman wears a fitted dress for dancing and necklaces of precious metals.
Traditional medicine is giving way to modern pharmacy.
Beauty and seduction depend on dance, elegance, adornments, work and cooking.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: koungouli (tam-tams that accompany the sultan), kolo, darmaiya, kaboul (birth of the Prophet), mile (dance reserved for princes).
Festivals: Mouloud, Tabaski, Ramadan; the cultural association AC Sao promotes the heritage.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Kotoko share many cultural traits with the Massa and the Mousgoum, who also claim descent from the Sao.

sections.title: The names
items: The sultan may give a name to those who do him a service.
The birth name does not change, but a title of office at the chiefdom is placed in front of it.
The founding ancestors are the Sao.

lessons.title: Who are the Kotoko (Kousseri)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Kotoko (Kousseri) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Kotoko (Kousseri) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Kotoko (Kousseri) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Kotoko (Kousseri) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Kotoko (Kousseri) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Kotoko (Kousseri) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Numerous group, mixed with the Massa, Mousgoum and other peoples of the town, to the point that it becomes difficult to tell them apart. • Shuwa Arabic serves as an indispensable lingua franca; Kotoko is also spoken at Magba and Lagdo. • Formerly mostly endogamous, the Kotoko now marry freely, men and women alike. • First occupants and founders of Kousseri, they regard themselves as the guardians of the town's traditions. • Coming from ancient Egypt via Sudan and Chad, they regard the Kotoko cities of neighbouring countries as their own.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Founders of Kousseri and guardians of its traditions, the Kotoko (Mantagé) say they are descended from the Sao, who came from ancient Egypt via Sudan and Chad. Under the authority of a sultan surrounded by notables, this people of Logone fishermen honours the water spirits, builds dugout canoes and dances to the sound of the sultan's drums.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Kotoko (Kousseri) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Kotoko (Kousseri)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Kotoko (Kousseri), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Kotoko (Kousseri), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Kotoko (Kousseri).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: okra, lalo, bocco (kalkouka). • Drinks: tea, porridge. • Activities: fishing, farming, market gardening.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kotoko (Kousseri) eat mainly okra, lalo, bocco. Traditional drinks: tea, porridge. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kotoko (Kousseri), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Kotoko (Kousseri). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Kotoko (Kousseri)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kotoko (Kousseri), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Kotoko (Kousseri). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kotoko (Kousseri), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Kotoko (Kousseri). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Worship of the water spirits: a black sheep is sacrificed to obtain an abundant catch and a safe crossing. • The appearance of the monitor lizard announces an event in the sultanate. • Symbolic places: the sultan's palace and court, the goudi (a pyramidal building that preserves traditions), the banks of the Logone, the Sao-Kotoko museum in Kousseri. • Birth is celebrated with a naming ceremony; “God created death before life”. • Murder is left to State justice; adultery brings a heavy fine.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cult of the water spirits: a black sheep is sacrificed to obtain an abundant catch and a safe crossing. The appearance of the monitor lizard announces an event in the sultanate.

steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Kotoko (Kousseri) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Kotoko
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Kotoko (Kousseri) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Kotoko (Kousseri) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Kotoko (Kousseri) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Kotoko (Kousseri) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Kotoko. • Greeting formulae: Baraku = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Okizu = morning greeting (one person); Ure kizu = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Sekeɗi, Kitcho, Kaker, kadé, Chéchi. • The founding ancestors are the Sao. • The Kotoko share many cultural traits with the Massa and the Mousgoum, who also claim descent from the Sao.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Kotoko are the first steps towards communicating with the Kotoko (Kousseri). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Kotoko are the first steps towards communicating with the Kotoko (Kousseri). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
